Per-assertion detail shows this isn't uniform: several individual assertions pass for both variants (e.g. "pre-provisioned capacity" and "actions for user not agent" in capacity-prewarm-focus; PASS/FAIL/N/A verdict formatting in full-readiness-eks-match and observability-third-party-alarms), some fail for both (e.g. "severity-ranked action plan tied to milestones" in full-readiness-eks-match, "CloudFront Functions vs Lambda@Edge" in cdn-origin-shield-audit, "states the FAIL rule for critical-path services" in observability-third-party-alarms) — these point to assertion- or behavior-level gaps affecting both variants rather than a between-variant difference. Many assertions are marked "flaky" (pass rate varies run to run within a variant), which tempers confidence in any single-run comparison. Confidence levels on expected-output and per-assertion judgments are mostly medium-to-high, though several key low-pass-rate assertions (e.g. in ivs-platform-applicability-gate, near-event-residual-risk) carry medium confidence, meaning the measurement itself is sometimes soft.

Quality comparison (LLM pairwise judging) could only be computed for a minority of pairs (most evals had 2-3 of 3 pairs skipped), so this dimension has limited coverage. Where available: cdn-origin-shield-audit favored with_skill (3-0 across criteria, medium confidence); mediatailor-ssai-and-drm-readiness favored without_skill (7-0, high confidence); capacity-prewarm-focus favored without_skill (2-0, medium confidence); observability-third-party-alarms was split/comparable (1-1-1). Runtime and cost consistently favor without_skill by a wide margin — without_skill typically runs in seconds to a couple minutes and costs cents to ~$1, while with_skill often runs several minutes (up to ~15m40s) and costs several dollars (up to ~$7.80), sometimes 10-20x more. In sum: with_skill tends to meet expected-output criteria and hit a broader set of assertions more often across most evals, but takes substantially longer and costs substantially more, and in a couple of evals (capacity-prewarm-focus, and partially mediatailor-ssai-and-drm-readiness quality judging) without_skill performed as well or was favored on quality/criteria despite much lower cost and runtime. **Overall picture:** The most substantive finding is the expected-output gap (with_skill meeting it in most runs, without_skill in none), paired with a large runtime/cost difference favoring without_skill. Assertions: Variant_a passed 7/8 (88%) individual assertions versus without_skill's 8/12 (67%), but the two variants were scored against different numbers of assertion instances (8 vs 12), reflecting differing run counts, so the raw pass-rate comparison should be read cautiously. Looking at the four distinct assertion types: two of them ("reactive autoscaling alone is insufficient..." and "presents pre-warm/reservation steps as user actions, not agent-made changes") passed 100% of the time for both variants — these are not differentiating and show both variants handle those aspects reliably. Another assertion (covering On-Demand Capacity Reservations, including future-dated reservations) was weak for both and notably weaker for without_skill: with_skill 1/2 (50%) and without_skill 0/3 (0%) — this looks like a genuine capability gap or an assertion/behavior that needs further work, since neither variant reliably satisfies it and without_skill fails it entirely.

Quality comparison: Only 1 of 3 pairs could be directly compared for quality (2 were skipped), so this comparison rests on very limited data. In that one evaluated pair, without_skill was favored overall and on accuracy and actionability, while completeness was rated comparable; confidence here is medium. Given only one comparable pair, this should be treated as a limited signal rather than a robust finding.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged 2m24s and $1.20 per run, while without_skill averaged 37s and $0.31 — without_skill was substantially faster and cheaper. One run exceeded a 30-second runtime threshold in the runtime comparison (high confidence), consistent with with_skill's longer average runtime. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (6.3% vs 5.1%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency: without_skill's outputs were rated consistent across repeated runs (score 3.0, high confidence) on all three dimensions checked. No consistency data was available for with_skill (marked null/absent), so no comparison can be made on this dimension — it is missing data, not a sign that with_skill was inconsistent.

Variant_b met the expected output more often and ran much faster and cheaper, with consistent outputs across runs. Variant_a had a higher raw per-assertion pass rate and performed better on the capacity-reservations assertion (though still imperfect), and did slightly better on the flaky warm-throughput assertion in raw pass rate (despite lower confidence than without_skill's score there). Assertion-level results show a split (one assertion favoring each variant, one failing for both), and several assertions are flagged as flaky, meaning the underlying behavior itself varies across runs for both variants. ivs-platform-applicability-gate.summary:
This eval tested how each variant handles a review scenario involving Amazon IVS (a service-managed/turn-key stack), checking whether the agent correctly treats AWS-managed primitives as N/A while still grading customer-managed portions, flagging gaps, and avoiding invented checks.

Trigger behavior: the behavior under test fired in all 3 runs (3/3) — this is a shared fact, not a point of difference.

Expected output: Neither variant met the expected output reliably. without_skill met it in 0/3 runs (0%), with high-confidence judgments, while with_skill met it in 1/3 runs (33%), with medium confidence. Both are low absolute rates, so the task as a whole appears to have been difficult for either variant to satisfy fully — this looks more like a shared challenge than a clear separation.

Per-assertion results: with_skill passed 4/8 assertion instances (50%), without_skill passed 4/12 (33%). Looking at individual assertions (all marked 'flaky' pattern, i.e. inconsistent across runs):
- Recognizing IVS as turn-key and marking AWS-managed primitives N/A: with_skill passed half the time, without_skill passed none of the time.
- Still grading customer-managed portions as PASS/FAIL/N/A rather than refusing: with_skill passed half the time, without_skill passed none of the time.
- Noting that full IVS review needs an IVS-specific skill: without_skill passed all instances (3/3), with_skill passed half (1/2) — here without_skill did notably better.
- Not inventing unverifiable IVS-specific checks: both variants passed only about half or a third of the time (with_skill 1/2, without_skill 1/3), suggesting this specific behavior is weak for both.
No assertion passed consistently for both or failed for both outright; results are mixed and inconsistent run-to-run for every assertion, which weakens confidence in any single-direction conclusion.

Metrics: without_skill was dramatically faster (~15s vs ~12m45s) and cheaper (~$0.13 vs ~$6.35) than with_skill, with slightly higher context utilization for with_skill (6.4% vs 4.7%). These are large, consistent differences in runtime and cost, though they must be weighed against the mixed/weak quality and expected-output results above — a faster, cheaper run is only a favorable tradeoff if output quality holds up, and here neither variant's output quality is strongly validated.

Quality comparison: no head-to-head quality pairs could be evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no direct quality comparison data available for this eval.

Output consistency: without_skill showed "mostly_consistent" behavior across repeated runs (score 2.33, medium confidence). No consistency data is available for with_skill (null), so no comparison can be made on this dimension.

Overall, this is a thin and mixed picture: both variants struggled to meet the expected output, assertion-level results vary by item (one assertion favors without_skill, two favor with_skill, one is weak for both), runtime/cost favor without_skill by a large margin, and quality-comparison and consistency data are incomplete or one-sided, limiting how confidently any overall difference can be drawn.
